title: “How Many Times?”
paragraphs:
“How Many Times?”
The Question Peter Asked That Exposed Every Wound We Hide—and the Grace That Refuses to Count
There are questions in Scripture that reveal more than curiosity.
Questions that sound simple on the surface but carry the weight of exhaustion, disappointment, betrayal, and pain underneath.
Peter asked one of those questions.
A question every parent has asked.
Every person who has ever been wounded by someone they loved.
The question was not merely about forgiveness.
It was about the moment when grace feels unfair.
It was about the point where mercy begins to feel impossible.
And if we're honest, it is still our question today.
"Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" (Matthew 18:21)
The apostle Peter was not asking as a theologian.
He was asking as a human being.
Because everyone eventually reaches a moment when forgiveness becomes expensive.
The third offense begins to harden the heart.
By the seventh offense, most people are already searching for the exit.
Peter likely thought he was being generous.
The rabbis of his day commonly taught forgiveness three times.
Peter doubled it and added one.
Surely God must have a limit.
In Greek, Matthew 18:22 records Jesus saying:
"οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις, ἀλλὰ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά."
(ou legō soi heōs heptakis, alla heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta)
Most English translations render this as:
"I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times" or "seventy times seven."
Jesus was not giving Peter a forgiveness spreadsheet.
He was destroying the very idea of keeping score.
Because the moment forgiveness becomes a calculation, grace has already disappeared from the equation.
And suddenly Peter's question becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us still keep score.
We remember the people who knew exactly where to wound us.
And every memory becomes another mark on an invisible ledger.
Yet secretly we are still counting.
That is why Jesus immediately tells a story.
A king settles accounts with his servants.
One servant owes an impossible debt.
The amount is almost beyond imagination.
It represented a debt that could never be repaid in multiple lifetimes.
The servant falls to the ground begging for mercy.
And the king does something shocking.
This scene carries extraordinary significance because Scripture repeatedly connects forgiveness with the cancellation of debt.
The Greek word often translated as forgiveness is "ἄφεσις" (aphesis).
But releasing someone from a debt they cannot repay.
And suddenly the story becomes personal.
Because before it is about forgiving others, it is about understanding what God has forgiven in us.
The Hebrew Scriptures anticipated this reality centuries earlier.
"As far as the east is from the west..."
"So far has He removed our transgressions from us."
The scandal of grace is that God does not merely tolerate repentant sinners.
This is why Christianity remains radically different from every system of self-salvation.
The Gospel does not begin with what we do for God.
It begins with what Christ has done for us.
At the cross, Jesus bore a debt He did not owe because we owed a debt we could never pay.
Because when Peter asked, "How many times?"
Jesus answered with the cross long before the cross happened.
The very man asking about forgiveness would soon need forgiveness beyond imagination.
In the darkest hours of Jesus' earthly ministry.
Can you imagine the weight Peter carried after hearing the rooster crow?
The certainty that he had ruined everything.
Perhaps Peter remembered his own question.
Perhaps he wondered if he had exceeded heaven's limit.
Perhaps he wondered if grace had finally run out.
And the risen Christ did not greet Peter with condemnation.
On the shores of Galilee, Jesus asked Peter three times:
Three opportunities to hear grace rewrite failure.
But that Jesus redeems what appears beyond redemption.
But that grace speaks a greater word.
But that Christ transforms scandals into testimonies.
Some readers know what it means to be wounded repeatedly.
Others know what it means to be the one who caused the wound.
Yet the invitation of Christ remains the same.
Because none of us arrived at salvation by deserving it.
"While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8)
The world asks, "What do they deserve?"
The Gospel asks, "What has Christ done?"
And every answer leads back to the cross.
Perhaps that is why Peter's question continues to echo across centuries.
Because it is not really about other people.
It is about whether we truly understand the mercy that saved us.
When we grasp the magnitude of our forgiven debt, extending grace becomes less about the other person's worthiness and more about Christ's sufficiency.
That does not mean abuse should be enabled.
It does not mean wisdom should disappear.
It does not mean boundaries are unbiblical.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not always identical.
Scripture teaches both grace and discernment.
But forgiveness always releases the right to personally collect the debt.
And in doing so, it liberates the heart of the forgiver.
Wondering how much longer you can endure.
Or maybe today you are the servant with the impossible debt.
Certain that you've gone too far.
Still proving that grace is greater than the worst chapter of your life.
And perhaps the greatest lesson hidden inside Peter's question is this:
The Kingdom of God is not built by people who never needed forgiveness.
It is built by people who received it and chose to give it away.
Maybe that's why this story refuses to leave us.
Because somewhere deep inside, every one of us is Peter standing before Jesus asking:
And every time, Christ answers with the same message:
"As many times as it took for Me to forgive you."
If this message stirred something deep inside you, don't let it stop here.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs today.
The people who changed history for Christ were rarely the people who never failed—they were the people who discovered that grace had the final word.
